terms.comment: To bring something out before people: books, witnesses, authorities, a person’s words. Its other common senses are to carry out, to stretch out, to put off (diem prōferre) and to make known (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: as he says (bringing in a quotation)
terms.grammar: phrase: put inside or after the quoted words
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 3.5: animusque aeger, ut ait Ennius, semper errat
terms.comment: The usual way to quote in Cicero: the words run on in his sentence and ut ait names their author.

terms.gloss: to cite (an author or witness as authority)
terms.comment: The old sense “to name” (Gell. 2.6.16); used of the person cited, not of the words. Its everyday sense is to praise (see praise).

terms.gloss: a passage (of a book), a quotation
terms.grammar: noun, second declension; plural locī in this sense
evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quōsdam trānsferam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A passage of an author has the plural locī, places loca (Lewis & Short); hence the house’s collections of locī classicī.

evidence: Quint. 2.15.24: ex Gorgiā Platōnis (Lewis & Short, s.v. excerpō)
terms.comment: A passage picked out of a book; to make extracts is excerpere (Cic. Inv. 2.4; Plin. Ep. 3.5.10, nihil umquam lēgit quod nōn excerperet).

terms.gloss: bring forward, adduce (a reason, an example)
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 4.3.23: quam causam afferam? (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: animusque aeger, ut ait Ennius, semper errat neque patī neque perpetī potest, cupere numquam dēsinit.
phrases.english: and a sick mind, as Ennius says, always wanders, can neither suffer nor endure, never stops wanting.

phrases.latin: et ego cautius posthāc historiam attingam tē audiente, quem rērum Rōmānārum auctōrem laudāre possum religiōsissimum.
phrases.english: and from now on I shall touch on history more carefully when you are listening, whom I can cite as the most scrupulous authority on Roman history.
